warnings: Cholinesterase inhibitors can cause bradycardia, heart block and syncope; check pulse before starting and after dose increases (heart rate 68 bpm at this visit).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Dysexecutive and behavioural impairment (disinhibition, utilization behaviour, failed go/no-go and motor sequencing) with impaired delayed recall on MMSE and MoCA, informant-confirmed decline over 18 months, and loss of instrumental independence (work, finances, meal planning)
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history, a per-domain profile and an explicit account of daily function
action_criteria.rationale: The patient minimizes her deficits, so the behavioural and executive syndrome and the loss of work and household function have to be documented with her husband before any cause is assigned [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe executive dysfunction (Trail Making B, WCST, Stroop, go/no-go) with impaired episodic memory (CVLT-3 delay 3/16) and a raised informant behavioural rating
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the executive, behavioural and memory profile and set a baseline
action_criteria.rationale: Quantified executive and memory testing shows whether episodic memory is involved alongside the frontal syndrome, which separates a dysexecutive Alzheimer presentation from pure bvFTD [bvAD_2015].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No reversible cause: TSH 3.2 on levothyroxine, B12, folate, homocysteine, electrolytes, renal and liver function normal
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: She takes levothyroxine, so thyroid replacement must be confirmed adequate, and B12, folate and metabolic causes excluded before a neurodegenerative diagnosis [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Frontal-predominant (left greater than right) atrophy with mild anterior temporal and hippocampal (MTA 2) atrophy; no mass or vascular lesion
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with a dementia protocol to define the pattern of atrophy and exclude a structural or vascular frontal lesion
action_criteria.rationale: A frontal behavioural syndrome at 58 needs MRI to exclude a frontal mass or vascular lesion and to show the regional atrophy pattern [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and here it decides between a frontal Alzheimer presentation and bvFTD, where cholinesterase inhibitors are not indicated [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bifrontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism with an additional posterior temporoparietal and posterior cingulate/precuneus component
action_criteria.label: Consider FDG-PET after the core assessment if the distinction from bvFTD remains uncertain
action_criteria.rationale: Posterior temporoparietal and posterior cingulate hypometabolism alongside the frontal deficit favours Alzheimer pathology over bvFTD [Foster_2007].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic variant in the frontotemporal dementia genes (C9orf72 repeat normal, GRN, MAPT) or in APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2
action_criteria.label: Offer genetic testing after pre-test counselling, covering frontotemporal dementia genes (C9orf72, GRN, MAPT) as well as APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2; do not use APOE as a diagnostic test
action_criteria.rationale: Onset at about 56 with a father and paternal uncle who had behavioural dementia makes a hereditary cause worth discussing, and the phenotype overlaps bvFTD, so an Alzheimer-only panel is too narrow [ACMG_NSGC_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No clinically significant interaction with buspirone, levothyroxine or sumatriptan; pulse 68 permits a start at 5 mg
action_criteria.label: Check interactions before starting donepezil
action_criteria.rationale: Before a cholinesterase inhibitor her buspirone, levothyroxine and sumatriptan should be reviewed and the resting pulse checked [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the behavioural change to depression or anxiety; it did not respond to sertraline or venlafaxine and is accompanied by frontal release signs and objective executive and memory deficits
Do not use antipsychotics for disinhibition or apathy; reserve them for severe distress or risk after non-drug measures, given the increased mortality in dementia [NICE_NG97]
Do not add a benzodiazepine for her anxiety, given the cognitive and fall risk [Beers_2023]
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; it is indicated for moderate or severe Alzheimer dementia [NICE_NG97]
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well; her own account minimizes the deficits
Disclose the diagnosis with her husband present, explain the expected course, and plan for durable power of attorney, advance directives and support for her husband
Protect her finances now: involve her husband in banking, set spending limits or remove card access for online purchases, and arrange financial power of attorney while she has capacity
Advise that she should not return to her role in banking and support a medical retirement or disability application; assess driving safety formally

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines, once Alzheimer pathology is supported, because cholinesterase inhibitors are not recommended in frontotemporal dementia [NICE_NG97].
Offer genetic testing only with pre-test and post-test genetic counselling; the result informs the family and not the patient's diagnosis [ACMG_NSGC_2011].
Use non-drug strategies for disinhibition and apathy (structured routine, supervised activities, caregiver education) and refer her husband to carer support

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

accepted: Frontal (behavioral/dysexecutive) variant of early-onset Alzheimer's disease

differential.key_features: Closest clinical mimic: early disinhibition, apathy, impulsive spending, executive dysfunction and frontal and anterior temporal atrophy meet the clinical features of bvFTD. Against it: early episodic memory impairment, posterior temporoparietal and posterior cingulate hypometabolism on FDG-PET, and amyloid positivity with raised p-tau181; biomarkers strongly indicative of Alzheimer disease are an exclusion criterion for bvFTD, and the FTD gene panel is negative

differential.diagnosis: Primary psychiatric disorder (late-onset mood or personality disorder)
differential.key_features: Against: no response to sertraline or venlafaxine, frontal release signs and utilization behaviour, objective executive and memory deficits, and frontal atrophy on MRI
No asymmetric rigidity, alien limb, supranuclear gaze palsy or postural instability
MRI shows only Fazekas 1 white matter change and no infarct; the course is gradually progressive
Light alcohol use without increase; buspirone, levothyroxine and occasional sumatriptan do not explain a progressive frontal syndrome

key_clinical_evidence: A behavioural or dysexecutive presentation of Alzheimer disease can mimic behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia; temporoparietal involvement on imaging and Alzheimer biomarkers separate them [bvAD_2015].
Early episodic memory impairment alongside a frontal behavioural syndrome should raise Alzheimer disease, and amyloid and tau biomarkers adjudicate the cause in such atypical presentations
Biomarkers strongly indicative of Alzheimer disease exclude a diagnosis of bvFTD under the international consensus criteria [FTDC_2011]
A family history of behavioural dementia does not establish frontotemporal dementia; when genetic testing is offered after counselling, it should cover the FTD genes as well as APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2

red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on familial bvFTD and skip Alzheimer biomarkers

metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Differentiating frontal variant AD from behavioral variant FTD in a patient with frontal-predominant behavioral and executive deficits, complicated by a family history suggestive of FTD
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, neuropsychological testing, the cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI. Optional: one amyloid biomarker test (CSF or amyloid PET), FDG-PET for the bvFTD question, counselled genetic testing (FTD genes or APP/PSEN1/PSEN2), and a donepezil interaction check.
metadata.educational_value: Teaches recognition of frontal variant AD as an atypical AD presentation that mimics bvFTD, and the critical role of AD biomarkers in differentiating these conditions
key_educational_points: Frontal variant AD can be clinically indistinguishable from bvFTD based on behavioral symptoms alone
Concurrent episodic memory impairment in a behavioral/dysexecutive presentation should raise suspicion for AD rather than pure FTD
FDG-PET showing posterior temporoparietal involvement in addition to frontal hypometabolism favors AD over FTD
Family history of behavioral dementia does not confirm FTD; familial AD can present with frontal symptoms
Negative FTD gene panel (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72) helps exclude genetic FTD but does not rule out sporadic bvFTD
Genetic testing is optional and requires pre-test counselling; APOE is not used to diagnose Alzheimer disease
One conclusive amyloid biomarker test (CSF or amyloid PET) is enough to establish amyloid status

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sofia Reyes is a 58-year-old right-handed bank branch manager who is referred to the neurology outpatient clinic by her primary care physician for evaluation of progressive behavioral changes and cognitive decline over the past 18 months. Her husband, who accompanies her, provides the majority of the history as the patient tends to minimize and joke about her difficulties. Approximately 18 months ago, her husband first noticed subtle changes in her personality. She began making inappropriate comments to colleagues and customers at the bank, including remarking on a customer's weight and making off-color jokes during staff meetings — behavior completely out of character for someone who had been known for her professionalism and interpersonal skills. Over the following months, she became increasingly apathetic, losing interest in activities she previously enjoyed including running, cooking, and socializing with friends. She has had progressive difficulty with organizational tasks at work — she was previously meticulous with documentation and compliance protocols, but began making errors in loan approvals, forgot to file regulatory reports, and could not manage multiple tasks simultaneously. Her judgment deteriorated — she made several impulsive online purchases totaling over $8,000 in a single month, bought items she already owned, and signed up for multiple streaming subscriptions she never used. After receiving formal complaints from three customers and two staff members about her inappropriate remarks, she was placed on medical leave 4 months ago. She was seen by a psychiatrist who diagnosed depression and tried sertraline 100 mg daily for 8 weeks, then switched to venlafaxine 150 mg for 6 weeks — neither improved her behavioral symptoms, and venlafaxine was stopped. Importantly, her husband reports that in addition to the behavioral changes, she has developed concurrent memory problems. She frequently forgets conversations from earlier in the day, repeats questions multiple times, forgets appointments despite using calendar reminders, and recently forgot that her daughter had visited the previous weekend. She also has difficulty learning new information — she could not figure out how to use a new coffee maker despite repeated instruction. She has not gotten lost but has had difficulty planning meals and following recipes she previously made from memory. She denies visual hallucinations, paranoid ideation, or delusional thinking. Sleep is unremarkable. There is no history of head trauma, seizures, or substance abuse. Her father's history of behavioral dementia beginning at age 70 is noted.
